edges.description: By reducing the acid barrier, PPI exposure lets a larger fraction of ingested Salmonella survive gastric transit to reach the intestine.
edges.source: Proton Pump Inhibitor Gastric Acid Suppression

edges.description: Organisms that survive gastric transit reach Peyer's-patch follicle associated epithelium and can bind GP2 on M cells through type 1 fimbriae.
Luminal Salmonella can directly invade enterocytes after SPI-1 type III secretion system assembly and effector translocation.
edges.target: SPI-1 Type III Secretion and Enterocyte Invasion

edges.description: M-cell uptake moves Salmonella across the epithelium, contributing to mucosal invasion that triggers acute intestinal inflammation.
SPI-1 translocation delivers SipB, which binds caspase-1 and activates IL-1β processing.
edges.source: SPI-1 Type III Secretion and Enterocyte Invasion

edges.description: SPI-1 translocation delivers SopB, which contributes to Salmonella-driven intestinal fluid secretion and inflammation.
edges.source: SPI-1 Type III Secretion and Enterocyte Invasion

edges.description: IL-1β signaling contributes to neutrophil recruitment into the infected distal bowel.
SopB contributes to the inflammatory component of Salmonella enteritis.
SopB-linked fluid secretion is one effector-level input into acute Salmonella diarrhea.
Neutrophilic mucosal inflammation and SopB-associated secretion generate the watery or inflammatory diarrhea of Salmonella gastroenteritis.
The inflamed gut oxidizes thiosulfate to tetrathionate, creating a respiratory electron acceptor that Salmonella can exploit anaerobically.
Respiratory growth in the inflamed lumen helps maintain high Salmonella burdens during acute transmissible enterocolitis.
Intestinal fluid secretion and exudation directly produce the high-volume loose stools that define the dominant Salmonella gastroenteritis symptom.
The acute inflammatory enterocolitis syndrome presents with fever in most culture-confirmed pediatric Salmonella gastroenteritis cohorts.
Inflamed ileocolonic mucosa and associated motility changes manifest as abdominal cramping and pain during acute Salmonella enterocolitis.
Mucosal inflammation and exudation sometimes make Salmonella diarrhea visibly bloody.
In a minority of patients, enteric infection progresses past the gut into bloodstream infection.

nodes.description: Salmonella uses type 1-pilus FimH to bind glycoprotein 2 on intestinal M cells, which can transcytose luminal bacteria into gut lymphoid tissue.

evidence.reference_title: Glycoprotein 2 (GP2): grabbing the FimH bacteria into M cells for mucosal immunity.
evidence.snippet: GP2 interacts with FimH, a major component of the type 1 pilus on the outer membrane of a subset of gram-negative enterobacilli such as E. coli and Salmonella enterica.

evidence.reference_title: RANKL is necessary and sufficient to initiate development of antigen-sampling M cells in the intestinal epithelium.
evidence.snippet: Sections of the intestinal wall taken 2 hours after the introduction of the bacteria revealed substantially enhanced uptake of both Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (35-fold) and Yersinia enterocolitica (46-fold) as a consequence of villous M cell induction by RANKL

nodes.description: SPI-1-dependent epithelial invasion and inflammatory signaling recruit neutrophils into the distal ileal and colonic mucosa, producing acute inflammatory enterocolitis.

evidence.reference_title: Salmonella SPI-1-mediated neutrophil recruitment during enteric colitis is associated with reduction and alteration in intestinal microbiota.
evidence.snippet: Large numbers of luminal neutrophils were observed in the ceca of WT-infected, but not in invAmut or ssaRmut infected mice.

nodes.description: About five percent of nontyphoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis cases progress to bacteremia, which can seed focal infections such as aortitis, endovascular infection, osteomyelitis, or meningitis.

evidence.reference_title: Non-typhoidal Salmonella aortitis.
evidence.snippet: Approximately 5% of patients with NTS gastroenteritis develop bacteremia and the incidence of extra-intestinal focal infection in NTS bacteremia is about 40%.

nodes.description: Proton-pump inhibitor use suppresses gastric acidity, weakening the stomach barrier that normally kills ingested Salmonella and raising susceptibility to Salmonella gastroenteritis.
nodes.id: Proton Pump Inhibitor Gastric Acid Suppression

evidence.reference_title: Use of acid-suppressing drugs and the risk of bacterial gastroenteritis.
evidence.snippet: gastric acid suppression induced by PPIs but not H2RAs is associated with an increased risk of Campylobacter and Salmonella GE.

evidence.reference_title: Systematic review: the use of proton pump inhibitors and increased susceptibility to enteric infection.
evidence.snippet: Severe hypochlorhydria generated by PPI use leads to bacterial colonisation and increased susceptibility to enteric bacterial infection.

nodes.description: Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 encodes a type III secretion system that injects Sip and Sop effectors into intestinal epithelial cells, rearranges the actin cytoskeleton, and drives enterocyte invasion.
nodes.id: SPI-1 Type III Secretion and Enterocyte Invasion

evidence.reference_title: Inhibition of the Type III Secretion System of Salmonella Enterica Serovar Typhimurium and Alleviation Pathogenicity Via Treatment with Xanthotoxol.
evidence.snippet: The Type III secretion system (T3SS) of Salmonella is a syringe-like protein injection apparatus that translocates bacterial effector proteins into host cells and is essential for epithelial invasion and early stages of pathogenesis.

evidence.reference_title: Minimal SPI1-T3SS effector requirement for Salmonella enterocyte invasion and intracellular proliferation in vivo.
evidence.snippet: Our results demonstrate the critical but redundant role of SopE2 and SipA for enterocyte invasion, prerequisite for transcriptional stimulation and mucosal translocation in vivo.

nodes.description: Moderate uncomplicated Salmonella gastroenteritis generally does not require antibiotics, but severe cases and high-risk patients are treated with active agents such as ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone.
nodes.id: Severe or High-Risk Case Antimicrobial Therapy

evidence.reference_title: [Bacterial diarrheas and antibiotics: European recommendations].
evidence.snippet: There is no argument to treat moderate salmonella gastroenteritis or carriage. However, the severe cases and those occurring in high risk patient must be treated (ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone).

nodes.description: Translocated Salmonella SipB binds host caspase-1, enabling cleavage and activation of pro-IL-1β as part of the early inflammatory response.

evidence.reference_title: Salmonella-induced cell death is not required for enteritis in calves.
evidence.snippet: SipB binds and activates caspase-1, which in turn activates the proinflammatory cytokine interleukin-1beta through cleavage.

nodes.description: The Salmonella SopB inositol phosphate phosphatase contributes to the intestinal fluid secretion and inflammatory response induced by S. Typhimurium in the ileal mucosa.

evidence.reference_title: Salmonella-induced cell death is not required for enteritis in calves.
evidence.snippet: The sopB mutant induced the same amount of TUNEL-positive cells as the wild type, but it was attenuated for induction of fluid secretion and inflammation.

nodes.description: Streptomycin-pretreated mice infected orally with S. Typhimurium model acute cecal and colonic inflammation and defined-microbiota studies test microbiota protection against systemic spread.

evidence.reference_title: Administration of defined microbiota is protective in a murine Salmonella infection model.
evidence.snippet: Infected mice receiving MET-1 lost less weight, had reduced serum cytokines, reduced NF-κB nuclear staining, and decreased neutrophil infiltration in the cecum.

nodes.description: Reactive chemistry in the inflamed intestine converts host thiosulfate to tetrathionate; S. Typhimurium then uses tetrathionate as an electron acceptor to respire ethanolamine and outgrow fermentative gut microbiota.

evidence.reference_title: Intestinal inflammation allows Salmonella to use ethanolamine to compete with the microbiota.
evidence.snippet: By inducing intestinal inflammation, S. Typhimurium sidesteps nutritional competition and gains the ability to use an abundant simple substrate, ethanolamine, which is provided by the host.
